glosses.body: The Arabic name of God — al-ilāh, "the God," contracted by long use. Pickthall keeps it untranslated throughout: not a different God but the Arabic-speaking Abrahamic name for the one God.

Ar-Raḥmān, ar-Raḥīm — both from the root r-ḥ-m, whose home meaning is the womb. Raḥmān names mercy as permanent nature; Raḥīm mercy in act, toward particular creatures. English needs two words where Arabic needs two intensities.
Rabb al-ʿālamīn. ʿĀlamīn is the plural of ʿālam — every created order at once: humans, jinn, all beings, all ages.

glosses.body: Māliki yawm ad-dīn. Dīn here means judgment, requital — the same word elsewhere rendered "religion"; the double sense is native to the Arabic.
Aṣ-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm. Ṣirāṭ is likely an old loan from Latin strata — a paved road — already naturalized in pre-Islamic Arabic.
Aḍ-ḍāllīn — wanderers from the way, the closing word of the sura as recited.

The muqaṭṭaʿāt, "disconnected letters" — three Arabic letter-names. Twenty-nine suras open with such letters; their meaning is genuinely unknown, and the classical commentators mostly let them stand as mystery. The reader meets, in the Qurʾān's second verse, a text announcing it will not explain everything.
Al-kitāb, "the Book" — the Qurʾān's name for itself here.
Al-muttaqīn, from taqwā — often "God-consciousness," a guarding attentiveness. The parenthesis is Pickthall's: "(evil)" is his supplement, not the Arabic's.
Al-ghayb — what lies beyond perception: the divine order, the hereafter, what no witness can attest.
Yuqīmūna aṣ-ṣalāh — the ritual prayer. Pickthall renders ṣalāh as "worship" throughout the translation; where he writes "worship," the Arabic names the five daily prayers.
Pickthall's parentheses mark his own insertions — words the Arabic implies but does not say. Here the unnamed addressee of "revealed unto thee" is made explicit.
